newsitem.title: USA: Analysts disappointed, not shocked by Alcoa.
newsitem.headline: Analysts disappointed, not shocked by Alcoa.

text.p: Wall Street analysts said they were mildly disappointed in the lower-than-expected third-quarter earnings posted Friday by Aluminum Co of America but conceded its earnings often are hard to predict because of the volatility of its pricing practices.
"It was moderately disappointing," said Richard Aldrich at Lehman Brothers. "But the metal price was plummeting (in the third quarter) so it's not surprising they came in below expectations."

Alcoa, the world's largest aluminum producer, posted earnings of $0.77 per share on an operating basis, compared with $1.27 last year. Wall Street's consensus estimate for the quarter was $0.95. Including a $65.6 million restructuring charge, Alcoa's earnings on a net basis were $0.39 per share for the third quarter. Revenues fell slightly to $3.2 billion from $3.3 billion.

Alcoa blamed weaker earnings on the charge and a 22-day strike at its Cleveland forging plant in September, which caused a $0.04 per share hit, as well as its marked-to-market contracts, which amounted to a $0.09 per share hit.
Alcoa adjusts the value of those contracts based on the current price for aluminum. Aluminum prices on the London Metal Exchange have been falling in recent months and fell sharply during September.
"Alcoa can be difficult to predict," Aldrich said. "With the marked-to-market contracts you have to predict the aluminum price on the last day of the quarter.
"(The earnings) are not shockingly surprising...the stock being down two and some change makes sense to me."
Alcoa shares fell 2-1/4 in midday trading on the New York Stock Exchange but were down one in late afternoon trade.

Chuck Bradford at UBS Securities said his estimate for the third quarter was $0.90. "I thought it could come in below my 90 cents, yes," he said. "The aluminum price was falling (in the quarter). Alcoa had to go into the commodity market and adjust prices."
But Bradford said he was surprised at the $6.8 million quarterly loss at Alcoa's Brazilian operation, an equity partnership plant.
That plant had made $7 million in the second quarter. "That plant should be making money," he said. "I think there might be a wrinkle there, but I can't say what it is."
Company officials were not available for comment.
